items.instruction:
Work in pairs. You will use the Prompt-Move Reference Card (mat-practice-move-card) and the practice transcript (mat-practice-annotation-transcript) together with the annotation worksheet (mat-worksheet-annotation).

Step 1 – Read the Prompt-Move Reference Card carefully. It defines five labels — INSTRUCTION, PRIMARY CONTENT, EXAMPLE, CUE and TEMPLATE — and explains how to tell text that is actually supplied to an AI tool (enacted) from text that only talks about doing so (mentioned).

Step 2 – Read the practice transcript all the way through. It is a fictional conversation between an adviser and a participant. All names, amounts and reference numbers in it are fictional.

Step 3 – Together, work through the annotation worksheet. For each line or group of lines in the transcript, decide whether a prompt move is being enacted in the text, merely mentioned or discussed, or is absent. Record your line numbers, label, quoted text and enacted-or-mentioned decision in the blank table on the worksheet. Do not pre-fill any row before discussing it with your partner.

Step 4 – Each partner notes, in their own section of the worksheet, which lines they personally annotated and their reasoning.

Step 5 – Discuss any lines where you and your partner reached different labels. Record whether you agreed, disagreed, or needed to revisit the card to check.

Step 6 – Answer the final question on the worksheet: which labels did your pair find absent from the transcript?

No AI tool is run during this activity. You are practising recognition, not generating output. This is formative rehearsal; no work is collected for evaluation or scoring.

items.instruction:
Work individually. You will use the construction worksheet (mat-worksheet-construction).

The worksheet gives you a fictional scenario: Willowmere Bike Repairs (fictional) needs to tell its customer Ashby Florists (fictional) that order ORD-305 (fictional) for two cargo-bike tyres, originally agreed for 17 June (fictional), will now arrive on 24 June (fictional). All these values are fictional.

Step 1 – Read the scenario on the worksheet and the guided steps.

Step 2 – Work through the guided steps to plan your prompt. Think about what task directive you want to give and which case details the AI would need.

Step 3 – Write your prompt in the blank drafting frame on the worksheet. Your prompt must include a visible task directive and the relevant fictional case details.

Step 4 – Add a fictional-data declaration. Either write one explicit statement that all details in your prompt are fictional, or attach a visible fictional label to every individual detail. Both routes are acceptable.

Step 5 – Work through the short self-check list at the bottom of the worksheet before you finish.

No AI tool is run during this activity. You write the prompt only; no generated output is needed or expected. Results would vary across models, contexts and runs, so inspecting any output would be a separate step. This is formative rehearsal; no work is collected for evaluation or scoring.

items.instruction:
Work individually, then with a partner. You will use the choice-explanation worksheet (mat-worksheet-choice-explanation).

Step 1 – Open the prompt you wrote on the Construction Worksheet (mat-worksheet-construction). Copy it into the space provided on the choice-explanation worksheet.

Step 2 – Read through your prompt and pick two distinct choices you made. A choice might be a word or phrase you selected, a detail you included or left out, the order in which you arranged information, or the level of specificity you used.

Step 3 – For each choice, quote the relevant wording from your prompt and write a short explanation of what you were trying to achieve or avoid with that choice. Use qualified language: describe what you hoped might happen or what you wanted to avoid, not what the choice guarantees. Results can vary depending on the model, the system context and other factors, and would need to be inspected.

Step 4 – Swap worksheets with your partner. Read their prompt and their two explanations. Write one question about each of their choices — something that prompts them to think further about what they intended.

Step 5 – Return the worksheets and read your partner's questions. You do not need to write answers now; the questions are for reflection.

No AI tool is run during this activity. You are working only with the prompt text you wrote. This is formative rehearsal; no work is collected for evaluation or scoring.

materials.title: Prompt-Move Reference Card
materials.content:
PROMPT-MOVE REFERENCE CARD

IMPORTANT NOTICE: The five labels below — INSTRUCTION, PRIMARY CONTENT, EXAMPLE, CUE and TEMPLATE — are an operator adaptation of prompt-construction concepts drawn from supported source material. This label set is not a validated or verbatim source taxonomy. The recognition illustrations use only the fictional business Lark Hill Pottery, which is declared fictional throughout. They do not use any facts from the practice transcript or the workshop scenario.

─────────────────────────────────────
KEY DISTINCTION: ENACTED vs MENTIONED

A prompt move is ENACTED when the text actually performs it — when the words are supplied directly to the AI tool as part of the prompt.

A prompt move is MENTIONED when the text only talks about the move — discussing, describing or suggesting it — without actually supplying it to the tool.

Example of the difference:
  Enacted: The prompt contains the words "Write a delivery-confirmation email to Lark Hill Pottery about order LHP-042 for two kiln shelves, dispatched 10 May." — These words are given to the tool.
  Mentioned: A speaker says "You could add the order number to the prompt." — This talks about adding a detail but does not supply it.

─────────────────────────────────────
LABEL 1 — INSTRUCTION

Definition: A direct directive telling the AI what action to perform. It names the task.

How to tell enacted from mentioned:
  Enacted — the imperative or directive sentence is present in the prompt text itself, addressed to the AI.
  Mentioned — someone describes or suggests giving the AI an instruction, without the instruction itself appearing in the prompt.

Recognition illustration (fictional business: Lark Hill Pottery — fictional):
  Enacted example: A prompt contains the sentence "Write a short email to Lark Hill Pottery confirming that their order of two kiln shelves has been dispatched." This sentence is the INSTRUCTION because it directly tells the AI what to produce.
  Mentioned example: An adviser says "You should start your prompt by telling the AI to write an email." This talks about giving an instruction but does not supply one.

─────────────────────────────────────
LABEL 2 — PRIMARY CONTENT

Definition: The specific information the AI should act on — the subject matter or data that the instruction applies to, such as a customer name, order reference, amount or date.

How to tell enacted from mentioned:
  Enacted — the specific details are present in the prompt text, supplied for the AI to use.
  Mentioned — someone refers to the idea of including details without actually providing them in the prompt.

Recognition illustration (fictional business: Lark Hill Pottery — fictional):
  Enacted example: A prompt contains "Customer: Lark Hill Pottery (fictional). Order reference: LHP-042 (fictional). Items: two kiln shelves. Dispatch date: 10 May (fictional)." These details are PRIMARY CONTENT because they supply the specific data the AI needs.
  Mentioned example: An adviser says "Make sure you include the customer name and order number." This mentions the idea of including details but does not supply them.

─────────────────────────────────────
LABEL 3 — EXAMPLE

Definition: One or more sample outputs (or input-output pairs) provided inside the prompt to show the AI the desired pattern or style. Supplying one example is called one-shot prompting. Supplying more than one is called few-shot prompting. Supplying no examples at all is called zero-shot prompting.

How to tell enacted from mentioned:
  Enacted — an actual sample message or sample output appears in the prompt text for the AI to learn from.
  Mentioned — someone discusses the idea of including an example, or describes what an example would look like, without actually providing one in the prompt.

Recognition illustration (fictional business: Lark Hill Pottery — fictional):
  Enacted example: A prompt contains "Here is a sample confirmation email for a different fictional customer: 'Dear Meadow Glass Studio, your order MGS-019 for three glass-blowing rods was dispatched on 8 May and should arrive within three working days. Many thanks, Lark Hill Pottery.' Now write a similar email for Lark Hill Pottery's order LHP-042." The sample email is an EXAMPLE (one-shot) because it is actually supplied in the prompt.
  Mentioned example: An adviser says "You could include a sample email to show the AI the style you want." This mentions the idea of an example but does not provide one; the prompt remains zero-shot.

─────────────────────────────────────
LABEL 4 — CUE

Definition: A leading word, phrase or partial sentence placed at the end of the prompt to nudge the AI toward a desired response format or opening. The AI is expected to continue from the cue.

How to tell enacted from mentioned:
  Enacted — the leading phrase or partial sentence appears as the final element of the prompt text, positioned for the AI to continue.
  Mentioned — someone describes or suggests using a cue without placing one at the end of the prompt.

Recognition illustration (fictional business: Lark Hill Pottery — fictional):
  Enacted example: A prompt ends with the words "Dear Lark Hill Pottery," as its final line. This is a CUE because it gives the AI a starting point to continue from.
  Mentioned example: An adviser says "You might end the prompt with the opening of the email to get the AI started." This mentions the technique but does not place a cue in the prompt.

─────────────────────────────────────
LABEL 5 — TEMPLATE

Definition: A reusable prompt structure containing clearly identified variable slots (placeholders) that can be replaced with specific data for different uses. Placeholders are typically shown in brackets or labelled slots, for example [CUSTOMER NAME] or [ORDER REFERENCE].

How to tell enacted from mentioned:
  Enacted — the prompt text itself contains bracketed or labelled slots intended to be filled in.
  Mentioned — someone describes the idea of a reusable structure or template without the prompt text containing actual placeholders.

A TEMPLATE illustration may contain clearly identified variable slots. When using a template for fictional scenarios in this workshop, substitute fictional details for each placeholder — for example, replace [CUSTOMER NAME] with a made-up business name. Do not substitute real customer details.

Recognition illustration (fictional business: Lark Hill Pottery — fictional):
  Enacted example: A prompt contains "Write a dispatch-confirmation email to [CUSTOMER NAME] about order [ORDER REFERENCE] for [ITEMS]. The order was dispatched on [DISPATCH DATE]. Sign off from Lark Hill Pottery." The bracketed slots are a TEMPLATE because they are placeholders for variable data.
  Mentioned example: An adviser says "If you want to reuse this prompt for different customers, you could turn it into a template with slots." This mentions the idea of a template but does not supply one.

─────────────────────────────────────
SUMMARY TABLE

Label          | Enacted when...                                      | Mentioned when...
INSTRUCTION    | Directive sentence is in the prompt text              | Speaker describes giving the AI a task
PRIMARY CONTENT| Specific details are supplied in the prompt text      | Speaker refers to including details without providing them
EXAMPLE        | A sample output appears in the prompt text            | Speaker discusses adding an example without providing one
CUE            | Leading phrase ends the prompt text                   | Speaker describes the technique without placing a cue
TEMPLATE       | Bracketed/labelled slots appear in the prompt text    | Speaker describes a reusable structure without slots

Zero-shot = no examples supplied. One-shot = one example supplied. Few-shot = more than one example supplied.
─────────────────────────────────────

citations.supported_claim: The corpus defines prompt construction as instruction plus primary content, describes examples (zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot), cues and templates as distinct prompt-construction moves, and recommends being descriptive and using examples; these concepts underpin the five labels and the enacted-versus-mentioned distinction on the reference card. Excerpt 7 explicitly distinguishes zero-shot (instruction, no examples) from few-shot (providing examples of desired output).

materials.title: Practice Annotation Transcript – Juniper Garden Centre and Northgate Dental Practice (fictional)
materials.content:
PRACTICE ANNOTATION TRANSCRIPT

OPENING NOTICE: This is a fictional practice transcript created for this workshop. All business names, customer names, reference numbers, amounts, dates and other details are entirely fictional. Juniper Garden Centre, Northgate Dental Practice, quote PR-112, EUR 128.50 and the date 21 June are all invented for practice purposes only. This transcript does not record a real conversation, a real AI session or any actual business transaction.

─────────────────────────────────────

1.  Adviser: Right, let's work through building a prompt together. We have a scenario: Juniper Garden Centre needs to send a message to Northgate Dental Practice about quote PR-112 for EUR 128.50 for a plant-care visit on 21 June. All fictional, of course.

2.  Participant: So we need to get the AI to write the message for us?

3.  Adviser: Exactly. Let's start with the simplest possible version and see what we have. Here's a first attempt: "Write an email to our customer about their quote."

4.  Participant: That's very bare. The AI won't know which customer, which quote, or what the visit is about.

5.  Adviser: You're right. So the next step is to add the specific details — the customer name, the quote reference, the amount, the date of the visit. Without those, the AI is working with very little to go on, and what it produces would need to be checked carefully before it could be used.

6.  Adviser: Watch this. New version: "Write a professional email from Juniper Garden Centre to Northgate Dental Practice regarding quote PR-112 for EUR 128.50 for a plant-care visit scheduled for 21 June. Ask the customer to confirm whether they would like to proceed."

7.  Participant: That's much more specific. It has the customer name, the quote number, the amount and the date.

8.  Adviser: Good. And notice I also told the AI what to do — write a professional email — and what to ask for at the end. Those two things are working together in that version.

9.  Participant: Could we make the tone more specific as well?

10. Adviser: Yes, we could add something about tone. For instance, we might say the email should be warm and professional. That kind of detail can shape what the AI produces, though results will vary depending on the model and the context, so you'd want to look at what comes back.

11. Adviser: Now, another thing you can do is add a sample message — an example of the kind of email you want — so the AI can see the style. If you give it one sample, that's one approach; if you give it more than one, that gives the AI more to work with. And if you give no sample at all, the AI relies entirely on the instruction and the details you've provided.

12. Participant: Do we need to include a sample every time?

13. Adviser: Not necessarily. It depends on how specific you need the style to be. For a straightforward business message, the instruction and the details are often enough to get something worth looking at.

14. Adviser: There's also another technique where you put a few words at the very end of the prompt to get the AI started. So instead of leaving the AI to decide how to open, you give it the opening yourself. For example, you might end the prompt with "Dear Northgate Dental Practice," and the AI continues from there.

15. Participant: So you're giving it the first line?

16. Adviser: Exactly. Here's the prompt with that ending added: "Write a professional email from Juniper Garden Centre to Northgate Dental Practice regarding quote PR-112 for EUR 128.50 for a plant-care visit scheduled for 21 June. Ask the customer to confirm whether they would like to proceed. Dear Northgate Dental Practice,"

17. Participant: And the AI just carries on from "Dear Northgate Dental Practice,"?

18. Adviser: That's the idea. It takes that opening and continues in that style. Whether it does so in a way that suits you depends on the model and the situation, so you'd check the result.

19. Adviser: Now, if you want something you can reuse for different customers and different quotes, you can build a structure with slots — placeholders you fill in each time. Something like this: "Write a professional email from [BUSINESS NAME] to [CUSTOMER NAME] regarding quote [QUOTE REFERENCE] for [AMOUNT] for [SERVICE DESCRIPTION] scheduled for [DATE]. Ask the customer to confirm whether they would like to proceed."

20. Participant: So we'd replace the bracketed parts with the actual fictional details each time?

21. Adviser: Exactly. The rest of the sentence stays the same; only the slots change. And when you use this in the workshop, fill in fictional details for each slot — made-up business names, fictional quote references, invented amounts. Do not use real customer details or real payment information.

22. Adviser: So in this session we've built a prompt that has a task directive, the specific case details, and a leading phrase at the end. We also talked about adding a sample message to show the AI the style, but we didn't actually put one into the prompt we built.

23. Participant: Could we have added a sample to make it stronger?

24. Adviser: Possibly. Adding a sample would give the AI a model to follow, which can sometimes help with style. But it also makes the prompt longer and more complex, and the effect would depend on the model. For a first attempt, keeping it simpler is often a reasonable starting point — then you can try variations and see what the results look like.

─────────────────────────────────────

citations.supported_claim: The corpus describes instruction, primary content, examples (zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot), cues and templates as distinct prompt-construction moves, and notes that model outputs are stochastic and require inspection; the transcript enacts and discusses these moves across numbered lines for learner annotation practice. Excerpt 6 supports the stochasticity and iteration framing used in lines 10, 18 and 24.

materials.title: Construction Worksheet – Construct a First Business Prompt
materials.content:
CONSTRUCTION WORKSHEET
Construct a First Business Prompt

FICTIONAL SCENARIO NOTICE: All business names, customer names, order references, dates and other details in this scenario are entirely fictional and are used for practice purposes only within this workshop.

─────────────────────────────────────
THE SCENARIO

Fictional business: Willowmere Bike Repairs
Fictional customer: Ashby Florists
Fictional order reference: ORD-305
Fictional items: two cargo-bike tyres
Original fictional agreed delivery date: 17 June
New fictional expected delivery date: 24 June

Willowmere Bike Repairs needs to send a message to Ashby Florists to let them know that order ORD-305 for two cargo-bike tyres, originally agreed for 17 June, will now arrive on 24 June. The message should be professional and apologetic in tone.

All values above are fictional.

─────────────────────────────────────
GUIDED STEPS

Step 1 — Task directive
What do you want the AI to do? Write a sentence that tells the AI clearly what to produce. Think about the type of message, the sender and the recipient.

Your notes:
_______________________________________________________________
_______________________________________________________________

Step 2 — Case details
What specific information does the AI need to write this message? List the details from the scenario that are relevant.

Your notes:
_______________________________________________________________
_______________________________________________________________
_______________________________________________________________

Step 3 — Tone and format (optional)
Do you want to specify the tone (e.g. apologetic, professional, brief) or the format (e.g. email, short note)? Note any preferences here.

Your notes:
_______________________________________________________________
_______________________________________________________________

Step 4 — Fictional-data declaration
You must include one of the following in your prompt:
  Option A: One explicit statement at the start or end of your prompt declaring that all business and customer details in it are fictional.
  Option B: A visible fictional label attached to every individual detail (for example: "Fictional customer: Ashby Florists").

Both options are acceptable. Which will you use?
  [ ] Option A — one overall declaration
  [ ] Option B — a label on every detail

─────────────────────────────────────
DRAFTING FRAME

Write your prompt in the space below. Include your task directive, the relevant fictional case details, and your fictional-data declaration or labels.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

─────────────────────────────────────
SELF-CHECK LIST

Before you finish, check each item below:

[ ] My prompt contains a visible task directive — a sentence telling the AI what to write.
[ ] My prompt includes the relevant fictional case details (customer name, order reference, dates, items).
[ ] My prompt includes either one overall fictional-data declaration OR a fictional label on every individual detail.
[ ] I have not included any real customer names, real order references or real payment details.
[ ] I have not run this prompt through any AI tool, and I am not expected to do so for this activity.

─────────────────────────────────────
REMINDER

No AI tool is run during this activity. You are writing the prompt only. If you were to run a prompt like this, results would vary depending on the model, the system context and other factors, and you would need to inspect what came back before using it. This is formative practice; no work is collected for evaluation or scoring.
─────────────────────────────────────

materials.title: Choice-Explanation Worksheet – Explain Two Prompt Choices
materials.content:
CHOICE-EXPLANATION WORKSHEET
Explain Two Prompt Choices

This worksheet asks you to look back at the prompt you wrote on the Construction Worksheet (mat-worksheet-construction) and explain two choices you made in it. You will then swap with a partner and ask each other one question per choice.

All details in your prompt should remain fictional, as required by the construction worksheet.

─────────────────────────────────────
STEP 1 — COPY YOUR PROMPT

Copy the prompt you wrote on the Construction Worksheet into the space below, exactly as you wrote it.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
│                                                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

─────────────────────────────────────
STEP 2 — IDENTIFY AND EXPLAIN TWO CHOICES

Read through your prompt and pick two distinct choices you made. A choice might be:
  • A word or phrase you selected
  • A detail you included or left out
  • The order in which you arranged information
  • The level of specificity you used
  • A tone instruction you added or omitted

For each choice, quote the relevant wording from your prompt and explain what you were trying to achieve or avoid. Use qualified language — describe what you hoped might happen or what you wanted to avoid, not what the choice guarantees. Results can vary depending on the model, the system context and other factors, and would need to be inspected.

CHOICE 1

Quote the wording from your prompt where this choice appears:
"_______________________________________________________________"

What were you trying to achieve or avoid with this choice?
_______________________________________________________________
_______________________________________________________________
_______________________________________________________________

CHOICE 2

Quote the wording from your prompt where this choice appears:
"_______________________________________________________________"

What were you trying to achieve or avoid with this choice?
_______________________________________________________________
_______________________________________________________________
_______________________________________________________________

─────────────────────────────────────
STEP 3 — PARTNER SWAP

Swap your worksheet with your partner. Read their prompt and their two explanations.

For each of their choices, write one question that invites them to think further about what they intended or what might happen differently with a different wording. Do not write an answer or a correction — just a question.

PARTNER'S NAME: ___________________________

Question about their Choice 1:
_______________________________________________________________
_______________________________________________________________

Question about their Choice 2:
_______________________________________________________________
_______________________________________________________________

─────────────────────────────────────
STEP 4 — RECEIVE YOUR WORKSHEET BACK

Read the questions your partner wrote about your choices. You do not need to write answers here. Use the questions as a prompt for reflection.

One thought the questions gave you:
_______________________________________________________________
_______________________________________________________________

─────────────────────────────────────
REMINDER

No AI tool is run during this activity. You are working only with the prompt text you wrote. Describing possible effects of your choices is appropriate; claiming that a choice guarantees a particular output is not, because results vary across models, contexts and runs and must be inspected. This is formative practice; no work is collected for evaluation or scoring.
─────────────────────────────────────
